```{r setup, include=F}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(psych)
source('_theme/theme_quarto.R')

theme_set(theme_quarto(title_font_size=42))
theme_update(
  text = element_text(family = 'Source Sans 3')
)

dapr3green <- "#88B04B" 
dapr3dkgreen <- "#5C7C28"
dapr3ltgreen <- "#E5EED7"
pal <- c( "#d35269", "#5c9ead","#2a3c24", "#F5C396", "#8B2635",  "#235789")



library(psych)
library(lavaan)
set.seed(346)
d1 <- simulateData("
f=~ 1*y1+1*y2+1*y3+1*y4+1*y5+1*y6
y1 ~~ 0*y1
y2 ~~ 0*y2
y3 ~~ 0*y3
y4 ~~ 0*y4
y5 ~~ 0*y5
y6 ~~ 0*y6
") |> apply(2,\(x) cut(x,7,labels=FALSE)) |> as.data.frame()

d2 <- simulateData("f=~ .8*y1+.8*y2+.8*y3+.8*y4+.8*y5+.8*y6") |> 
  apply(2,\(x) cut(x,7,labels=FALSE)) |> as.data.frame()

# set.seed(533612)
set.seed(9935)
d3 <- simulateData("f=~ .8*y1+.8*y2+.8*y3
                   f1=~.8*y4+.8*y5+.8*y6
                   f~~.5*f1") |> 
  apply(2,\(x) cut(x,7,labels=FALSE)) |> as.data.frame()

names(d1) <- names(d2) <- names(d3) <-
  c("dgstv","hbnb","rcht","oreo","brbn","choclbnz")

d3a <- d3 |> mutate(f1 = rowMeans(pick(dgstv:rcht)),
                    f2 = rowMeans(pick(oreo:choclbnz))) |>
  mutate(across(f1:f2,~cut(.,5,labels=F)))

d1 <- d1 |> mutate(ppt=paste0("PPT",1:n()),.before=dgstv)
d2 <- d2 |> mutate(ppt=paste0("PPT",1:n()),.before=dgstv)
d3 <- d3 |> mutate(ppt=paste0("PPT",1:n()),.before=dgstv)

```

# overview

- problem: too many variables
- what: reduce
- how: pca/efa

## starting point

- measurement is difficult, and often introduces error.   

- especially in psychology, we might use "multi-item measures" (n different "tests" of the same thing)

:::{.fragment}

- necessary because:
    - constructs are multi-faceted
    - individual tests have noise/error

:::

## therefore...

- increased "dimensionality"

- more columns in our data, but they all kind of mean the same thing. 

## example

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
we get people to answer 6 questions rating how much they like:  

- dgstvs
- hobnobs
- rich tea
- oreos
- bourbon
- choc-leibniz
  
for each Q, people rate it 1-7


:::
:::{.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
set.seed(345)
d1 |> 
  slice_sample(n=10) |>
  mutate(across(2:7, ~"---")) |>
  gt::gt()
```

:::
::::


## the idea of reducing

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}

- our variables all measure the same thing (love of biscuits)
- can we express this information more efficiently? 
    - i.e. *without* having to use all 6 variables?  


:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
set.seed(345)
d1 |> 
  slice_sample(n=10) |>
  mutate(across(dgstv:`choclbnz`, ~"---")) |>
  mutate(`(unobservable) love of biscuits`="??") |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_style(
     style = gt::cell_text(color = "grey70"),
     locations = gt::cells_body(columns = 8) 
   ) 
```
:::
::::


## a perfect world

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}

- if the *only* reason people differ on these variables is because of "how much they like biscuits", then each Q is a perfect measure of that, and we might see:

:::
:::{.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
set.seed(345)
d1 |> 
  slice_sample(n=10) |>
  gt::gt()
```

:::
::::


## a perfect world

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}

- if the *only* reason people differ on these variables is because of "how much they like biscuits", then each Q is a perfect measure of that, and we might see:

:::
:::{.column width="50%"}

```{r}
d1 |> select(-ppt) |> cor()
d1 |> select(-ppt) |> plot()
```

:::
::::






## a perfect world

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}

Can we express this information more efficiently? (can we "reduce"?)  

:::{.fragment fragment-index=1}
yes!  

- "people either score 1 on all 6 Qs, or 2 on all 6 Qs, or 3.."   

:::

:::{.fragment fragment-index=2}

^ one dimension, captures everything

:::

:::
:::{.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
set.seed(3446)
slice_sample(d1,n=6) |>
  gt::gt()
```

:::
::::


## a perfect world

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}

- whatever we do (PCA, EFA, take a mean/sum score), reducing down to 1 thing would capture 100% of the variance - we wouldn't lose _anything_  



:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r}
d1 |> select(-ppt) |> scree()
```
:::
::::

## reality

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}

- in reality, measures aren't perfect.  

- "do you like hobnobs?" isn't a perfect measure of someone's love of biscuits in general.  


:::
:::{.column width="50%"}


```{r}
#| echo: false
set.seed(35)
bind_rows(
  d2 |> mutate(f1 = rowMeans(pick(dgstv:`choclbnz`))) |> 
    arrange(f1) |> select(-f1) |> slice(1:2),
  slice_sample(d2, n=2),
  d2 |> mutate(f1 = rowMeans(pick(dgstv:`choclbnz`))) |> 
    arrange(desc(f1)) |> select(-f1) |> slice(1:2),
) |> gt::gt()
```

:::
::::




## scenario 1

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}

If there is thing that these items all share, we can still express the information with less (we can still "reduce").  

:::{.fragment fragment-index=1}
e.g.:  

- "people tend to be high on all 6 Qs, medium on all 6, low on all 6" 

:::

:::{.fragment fragment-index=2}

^ one dimension, captures a lot of "why people score high/low" on individual questions

:::

:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
set.seed(35)
bind_rows(
  d2 |> mutate(f1 = rowMeans(pick(dgstv:`choclbnz`))) |> 
    arrange(f1) |> select(-f1) |> slice(1:2),
  slice_sample(d2, n=2),
  d2 |> mutate(f1 = rowMeans(pick(dgstv:`choclbnz`))) |> 
    arrange(desc(f1)) |> select(-f1) |> slice(1:2),
) |> gt::gt()
```

:::
::::


## scenario 1

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}

- all the variables correlate at a similar level with all the others  

- 1 dimension captures most of the variance

:::{.fragment style="font-size:.8em"}

what information do we lose?  
there are 5 other dimensions that don't explain anything shared across questions:  

- some people have a specific preference/dislike for digestives
- some people have a specific preference/dislike for hobnobs 
- some people have a specific preference/dislike for rich tea
- ...
- ...

:::

:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r}
d2 |> select(-ppt) |> cor() |> round(2)
d2 |> select(-ppt) |> scree()
```
:::
::::

## PCA and EFA

PCA & EFA are about reducing to new dimensions without losing too much

- the only real differences:
    - conceptual: is the dimension a "common cause" (EFA) or a "summary composite" (PCA)
        - if a "common cause" then we need it to be theoretically meaningful
    - practical: do we want to let these new dimensions be correlated? (EFA, rotated)

## scenario 1 - EFA

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}


- if there's just 1 thing driving 'why people score high/low on these questions'?, and everything else is specific preferences for specific biscuit types... then 

- the 1-factor model will look best
- if we try to add more factors, we just end up with factors that have only 1 item. 
    - this isn't helpful - these factors don't give us something 'shared'. they just give us the hobnob-specific variation. we're not reducing anything.   

:::
:::{.column width="50%" .fragment}

```{r}
fa(d2[,-1],nfactors=2,rotate="oblimin")$loadings |> 
  print(cutoff=.3)
```


:::
::::


## scenario 2 - what if.. 

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}

- what if there's another useful dimension?  

- in other words: what if there's not just 1 thing driving 'why people score high/low on these questions'?  

:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
__\*different data\*__
```{r}
#| echo: false
bind_rows(
  d3a |> arrange(f1,f2) |> select(-f1,-f2) |> slice(1:2),
  d3a |> arrange(f1,desc(f2)) |> select(-f1,-f2) |> slice(1:2),
  d3a |> arrange(desc(f1),f2) |> select(-f1,-f2) |> slice(1:2),
  d3a |> arrange(desc(f1),desc(f2)) |> select(-f1,-f2) |> slice(1:2)
) |> 
  mutate(
    `unobserved thing 1` = "??",
    `unobserved thing 2` = "??"
  ) |>
  gt::gt() |>
    gt::tab_style(
     style = gt::cell_text(color = "grey70"),
     locations = gt::cells_body(columns = 7:8) 
   ) 
```



:::
::::

## it's all in the correlations

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}

there are patterns in the correlation matrix.  

:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r}
d3 |> select(-ppt) |> cor() |> round(2)

d3 |> select(-ppt) |> cor() |> heatmap()
```
:::
::::

## more than 1 dimension

```{r}
d3 |> select(-ppt) |> scree()
```

## scenario 2 - EFA

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
just 1 factor explains 27%
```{r}
fa(d3[,-1], nfactors = 1, rotate = "oblimin")
```
:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
2 factors explains 37%
```{r}
fa(d3[,-1], nfactors = 2, rotate = "oblimin")
```
:::
::::

## scenario 2 - EFA

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
Allowing our dimensions to be correlated, we get a nice clean pattern:  
Why do people differ on these 6 Qs?  

1. it partly depends on whether they like/dislike non-chocolatey biscuits
1. it partly depends on whether they like/dislike chocolatey biscuits

and these two dimensions are correlated - if you like non-chocolatey, typically you like chocolatey!  
  
:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
```{r}
fa(d3[,-1], nfactors = 2, rotate = "oblimin")$loadings |>
  print(cutoff = .3)
```
:::
::::


## 

- because the 2 factors correlate, their combination explains variance.
- if we force orthogonal/no rotation (i.e. zero correlation), this variance gets shoved into the loadings
- results in cross loadings and makes the factors more difficult to define. 

```{r}
fa(d3[,-1], nfactors = 2, rotate = "varimax")
```
